newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grains - Indonesia on corn-buying spree.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grains - Indonesia on corn-buying spree.

text.p: Indonesian feedmills are believed to have locked in some 400,000 tonnes of mostly U.S. corn for delivery in the second quarter of 1997, traders said on Wednesday.
"At least six Panamax vessels are due in the second quarter," one trader in Indonesia said. "In the first quarter, imports were around 180,000 tonnes."
He said the Panamax cargoes were quoted around US$145 a tonne C&F, while Argentine corn was being offered at $155 a tonne C&F for Handy-sized vessels.

Another dealer said local demand for corn was strong, with the harvest in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra proceeding unhindered. Local prices were generally stable at 390 rupiah a kg, unchanged from a week ago.
Traders said demand for soymeal was also robust, with prices seen rising in the near term. Local prices had climbed to 810-820 rupiah a kg from last week's quote of 780 rupiah.
One trader said India origin soymeal was being offered at $316-$318 a tonne CIF, but added that the country only had about 600,000 tonnes available for exports until October.

"The amount is nothing compared with Far East and Southeast Asian demand of 400,000 tonnes per month," he said. "I think India will not sell anything after April, as it holds back until prices peak in the third quarter."
The rest of the grains and oilseeds market in Southeast Asia was quiet, regional traders said.
In Malaysia, consumer demand did not emerge as expected despite the end of the long Lunar Chinese New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr holidays earlier this month.
Traders said the market had ample spot stocks of corn and other grains, but buyers were looking for some forward supplies.

"It's pretty much the same...sellers are desperately trying to offload tonnes of spot maize (corn), but few are interested in buying as warehouses are full and there's no storage space," said the manager of a flour mill in Kuala Lumpur.
A trader said importers were looking to secure Chinese corn at around $150 a tonne C&F for March/April shipment.
A trading source said Federal Flour Mills Bhd and several other major importers were scouting for about 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes of Chinese corn.
"People are dealing directly with Hong Kong to buy the Chinese maize as there's no one selling forward locally," the source said.
China's official agency for commodities said in Kuala Lumpur that it had no orders lodged for spot corn this week.
The price of bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, was at 390-395 ringgit a tonne this week.
"A" grade wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown in the central region, was at 750 ringgit a tonne.
The price of low-grade wheat, also centrally-based, was indicated around 450 ringgit a tonne.
Imported soymeal was at 820 ringgit, while the local material was seen at 810 ringgit, both in the central region.
The Thai grain and oilseeds market was also dull this week as buyers were sidelined by recent high world prices, trade sources said.
Import activity was thin. The prices of soymeal and corn in the local market rose because of tight supplies, they said.
But traders expected buying to emerge if prices continue to ease after the U.S. Agriculture Department released its latest crop estimate on Monday.
"The prices eased...due to the news. If they continue their downward momentum a bit, buyers could enter the market again very soon," said one dealer from a U.S. trading house.
One major oil crusher expressed interest in buying around 50,000 tonnes of soybeans but had not concluded the deal due to high prices.
A tight soymeal supply situation was partly alleviated by arrivals from India and product crushed from recently imported beans by oil crushers.
Soymeal prices were quoted around 9.60 baht a kg from 9.55 baht last week. Brisk buying pushed the domestic corn price up to 4.50 baht a kg from 4.38-4.40 baht last week.
Traders said the Thai Commerce Ministry should come up with details of the zero-tariff scheme for corn imports soon as local stocks were being depleted.
Thai industry sources projected that they would need to import up to 400,000 tonnes of corn this year.
